page: Amazon Web Services x8aedz.xlarge is a memory-optimized instance operating on the AWS Nitro System. It is powered by an AMD EPYC 9R05 processor featuring 4 dedicated physical cores and 4 vCPUs at a clock speed of 5.0 GHz. Designed for extreme memory density, it pairs these 4 cores with 128.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory (6 GHz), yielding an expansive ratio of 32.0 GB of RAM per core. The instance is bundled with 316 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and provides a baseline network throughput of 3 Gbps, with zero integrated GPUs.

Benchmark results demonstrate exceptional single-thread performance, driven by the 5.0 GHz AMD core architecture. In single-core testing, the instance scores in the top tier for stress-ng (4198.79) and Geekbench (3081.0), with single-threaded compression and decompression tests also attaining top-tier ranks (gzip compression reached 45.65 GB/sec). Multi-core benchmarks such as stress-ng multi-core (16770.34) and Geekbench multi-core (9701.0) fall squarely into average tiers, directly reflecting the low overall core count of 4 vCPUs. Memory benchmarks show large-block read bandwidth of 99.66 GB/sec and write bandwidth of 68.3 GB/sec, supporting fast throughput to local memory arrays.

The primary tradeoff of the x8aedz.xlarge instance lies in its compute capacity versus memory scale. While individual cores perform at the top tier, total aggregate parallel compute is limited by the 4-core configuration. When executing larger machine learning workloads, inference performance degrades severely; for instance, LLM prompt processing on a 70B parameter model registers in the bottom 10% (3.48 tokens/sec). Conversely, smaller language models and in-memory key-value processing thrive, as shown by Redis reaching 16.72 million SET operations per second and small model text generation achieving 443.36 tokens/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the instance is targeted at memory-heavy workloads that do not require broad multi-threaded CPU footprints. Providing 128 GB of DDR5 alongside local NVMe storage on only 4 vCPUs prevents organizations from over-provisioning unused CPU cores solely to obtain adequate memory capacity. The instance is well suited for in-memory caching solutions like Redis, single-node transactional databases, memory-bound data transformations, and applications requiring strong single-thread performance alongside massive RAM.
